CS201 and 202 are courses that make you hate the department with all your heart. And that hatred is justified. The curriculum is somewhat okay; it definitely has points for improvement, but they are not that important. Here are the real problems with the course.
Firstly, homework was NOT prepared well. When I say NOT, I really mean it. They were like they were written by AI, with 0 checks after. In one of the homework assignments, one of the outputs was wrong, and when we asked about that, he said HE DOES NOT HAVE A SOLUTION CODE AND HE HAS WRITTEN THE OUTPUTS BY HAND. I can not accept that a TA can say this to students who are doing his homework. Homework topics were good, but execution was not any better than terrible. About the exams, they were not designed to measure the understanding of the course; it was basically trying to reduce grades based on random things they have on paper. For a course focused on algorithm design, giving like 1-2 points out of 20 when there is a simple bug caused by writing on paper but giving half of the points when the design is completely wrong is not logical. The only explanation is that the lack of quality in the exam is causing a random grading criteria to get a reasonable grade distribution. Many students are getting worse grades for these trivial reasons in a course called Fundamentals of Computer Science, which will heavily affect how their transcript looks and probably ruin their academic career. Instructors need more awareness about the importance and state of the course. By saying this, I mean no disrespect. I am grateful to them for their efforts in teaching and education. But this course has serious problems, and I hope they can be fixed in the future.

It is hard for me to come up with any upsides of this course. I will explain why, in case anyone reads this.

The first part of the course is concerned with formal description of syntax, and the basics of parsing. We learn about two programs, lex and yacc. A lot of time is spent on the specification syntax of these two programs, something which can be given as a reading assignment almost. A bigger issue is that we don't learn any theory that makes these two programs possible, we cover them extremely superficially (no regex FSM construction, LR parsing). This causes major confusion when we examine parser conflicts, even amongst instructors. 

The second part of this course (which has no connection to the first part) is obsessed with the syntax of imperative languages. 3rd year CS students are already extremely familiar with the imperative programming paradigm. In the lectures, instructors frequently say "you are already familiar with this" etc... This causes extremely boring lectures which is honestly impossible for some students to follow. We mention functional programming in the last week, something almost no students are familiar with and an honest opportunity to learn something new.

I will end with two proposals on how to improve the syllabus:

1) Keep the first part of this course, add sections on the theory of parsing and regex, and move towards a course on compiler design. It might make sense as the students took "Computer Architecture" last semester.

2) Remove the first part of this course (at least the lex-yacc cycle and project 1-2, maybe keep BNF),  and reduce the time spent on imperative. Add more sections on functional programming and logic programming, maybe even something like Lean. Examine the applications of these paradigms. This gives us more opportunities to learn something new.

If you want further feedback from me on this course, shoot an email to this section, I will reply to it. I have more to say but I am limited by the character limit.
